Breaking Bread: How We Find Our Way Back to Civility | David Beasley | TEDxFargo
recentItems.description:
What if the simplest way to bridge our deepest divides is to sit down and share a meal?

After years working on the front lines of global hunger as Executive Director of the United Nations World Food Programme, David Beasley learned that food can do more than sustain us. It can bring people together.

From war zones and famine to the growing divisions in American public life, Beasley reflects on what happens when we remember our shared humanity. He challenges us to look beyond politics, ideology, and differences, and to make time for genuine conversation with people who see the world differently.

His invitation is simple: break bread with someone from a different background, culture, political party, race or generation.. Listen. Connect. Find the common ground. That is the pathway back to civility.

Because America's greatness, he argues, is tied to its goodness, and rebuilding that goodness starts with each of us. David Beasley, a former Governor of South Carolina, recently served as the Executive Director of the World Food Programme (WFP), having been nominated by two President’s Administrations of two different parties and appointed to that role initially in 2017 by the UN Secretary-General of the United Nations and served until April 2023.

Under Mr. Beasley’s leadership, WFP was the largest humanitarian organization in the world assisting over 160 million people in 2022 alone and raising over $55 billion USD.

In 2020, Mr. Beasley received the Nobel Peace Prize on behalf of WFP for its efforts to provide food assistance in conflict areas and to prevent food from being used as a weapon of war and conflict. In his acceptance speech delivered in Oslo on December 10, 2021,

Mr. Beasley stated that “Working with 115 million people in 80 countries, day-in and day-out, the women and men of WFP have gained a unique perspective. We have learned that there is great richness in those who are seen, in the eyes of the world, as “the poor.” And many of us who are considered “rich” are actually poor in the things that matter most.” Mr. Beasley also received the John F. Kennedy Profiles in Courage Award for his stand on the Confederate Flag as well as many other awards. He majored in Microbiology at Clemson University and received a Doctor of Jurisprudence degree from the University of South Carolina. He also was a Fellow and taught at the Harvard University Kennedy School of Government. He is married to the former Mary Wood Payne and is the father of four children and three grandchildren. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Shakespeare Still Has Bars | Sonnet Man, Devon Glover | TEDxFargo
recentItems.description:
What if Shakespeare's words were meant to be heard as rap?
The Sonnet Man brings Shakespeare to life through an energetic fusion of classic text and original hip-hop. From the enduring questions of love in Sonnet 116 to the existential struggles of Hamlet, he transforms Shakespeare's language into music while revealing just how modern these ideas still feel.
He closes with an excerpt from Julius Caesar, celebrating Shakespeare's lasting influence on the English language, and the countless phrases, words, and ideas we still use today. Shakespeare wrote for an audience. The Sonnet Man shows us why that audience could still be us. Devon Glover, known worldwide as The Sonnet Man, is a Brooklyn-based rapper, poet, teaching artist, musician, and arts educator who brings Shakespeare to life through Hip Hop. For more than two decades, Devon has used music and poetry to make classical literature accessible, relevant, and exciting for new audiences.

As The Sonnet Man, Devon performs Shakespeare’s sonnets in their original form before transforming them through original Hip Hop, revealing the rhythm, emotion, and contemporary relevance within Shakespeare’s language. He has performed and led thousands of workshops across more than 40 U.S. states, four continents, and more than 20 countries.

A graduate of Ithaca College, Devon has worked as a rapper, poet, director, sound designer, and text coach, creating original work for organizations including Flocabulary, Arts Partners, Southern Shakespeare Company, Shakespeare Behind Bars, and Salty Shakespeare. He is a patron of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, an associate member of the Shakespeare Theatre Association, and a longtime teaching artist and arts advocate.

Devon was featured on NBC’s Today Show, bringing national attention to his innovative approach to Shakespeare. At the heart of his work is a simple belief: everyone has a unique voice and a story worth sharing—and sometimes the best way to discover it is to find your own rhythm. recentItems.title: This tree's returns outperform VC funds. Why it is disappearing? | Matthew Ross | TEDxBoston
recentItems.description: Well, money doesn't technically grow on trees, but wealth does. One coconut palm, planted in the ground for 60 years, produces 57 marketable products — from water and oil to biochar, rope, and carbon credits — at a 168% compound annual growth rate that outperforms most venture capital funds. The problem is that the trees and the farmers who tend them came of age at the same time, about 60 years ago, and both are now disappearing together. Coconut water that costs five dollars today could cost fifty in a decade if no action is taken. Not because of market forces, but because the source trees and the people who grow them are literally vanishing. Across 27 million hectares of tropical coastline, the opportunity to restore that system and build the wealthiest portfolios on Earth is still there. But the window is closing fast. Watch the talk to find out how. Matthew Ross is the founder of a tropical agroforestry enterprise working to restore and expand coconut farming across 27 million hectares of coastline and island communities in South and Southeast Asia, building biodiverse multi-species portfolios that he calls coconut portfolios. With a background in entrepreneurship and community development, he spent years living and working in rural coconut-farming villages in the Philippines, where he observed firsthand the twin crises of aging farmer populations and aging coconut trees threatening to collapse a $10 billion global market. He argues that the coconut palm is the world's wealthiest tree, producing 57 marketable products over a 60-year lifespan, and that reconnecting trees and farmers to biodiverse community-based systems is the path to both ecological restoration and rural economic renewal. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: We all win when we care for the people caring for our rainforests | Kinari Webb | TEDxBoston
recentItems.description: Deforestation is a scourge that compounds dire climate stress across the planet. How do we stop the destruction? It turns out, we can start by radically listening. The stressors on the planet's systems are often deeply interconnected to stressors within the local indigenous communities that have been guardians of their home forests for generations. A man who spent his life protecting his rainforest made a deal with illegal loggers when his child got sick. A widow in Madagascar cleared land critical for lemurs to feed her ten children. What do we expect of people forced to choose between survival of their family or their forest? When that impossible choice is allieviated, they choose both. Their tending creates tangible value enjoyed across the world. By asking communities what they actually need, then building clinics, livelihoods, and education systems that support stewards, forest destruction becomes unnecessary. In just one community, the results: 90% fewer households logging, infant mortality down 67%, and a 12-to-1 return on investment in averted carbon loss. It all begins with recoprocity.  Dr. Kinari Webb is a physician and the founder of Health In Harmony, a nonprofit that has protected more than 20 million acres of rainforest in Indonesia, Madagascar, and Brazil by addressing the human health needs that drive deforestation. She first went to Borneo as a primatology student, then returned as a doctor, founding a community health clinic in one of the most biodiverse regions on Earth. She holds a medical degree from UCLA and a master's in public health from UNC Chapel Hill. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Breaking the blueprint of patriarchy | Hafidha Abass | TEDxMiddlesex University Mauritius
recentItems.description: What begins as a reflection on childhood quickly becomes a powerful conversation about gender and identity. Hafidha explores how girls are often shaped by societal expectations that dictate how they should behave, dress, and dream. By unpacking these deeply rooted stereotypes, she challenges the audience to rethink traditional norms and embrace actions that help break the cycle of patriarchy. Through awareness and everyday choices, she shows how meaningful change starts with each of us. recentItems.title: What’s the point of university strategies? | Shân Wareing | TEDxMiddlesex University Mauritius
recentItems.description: Professor Shân Wareing shares an engaging perspective on why strategies are often misunderstood, arguing that while bad strategies can create confusion and stagnation, good strategies have the power to drive meaningful transformation. Using examples from higher education, she explores how organisations must adapt to change while staying focused on long-term goals and financial sustainability. The talk highlights the importance of aligning people, resources, and priorities around a shared vision rather than creating unrealistic wish lists.  Professor Shân Wareing took up her position as the Vice-Chancellor of Middlesex University in April 2024. She is Chair of the charity, Unite Foundation, Chair of Advance-HE’s Leadership and Management Strategic Advisory Group, and Co-Chair of the Advance HE Leadership Framework Steering Group. She has published in the fields of linguistics, equality, diversity and inclusion, leadership and team development, and learning and teaching in higher education. Her current scholarly interests are university leadership and governance from the perspective of diversity and inclusion, digital transformation, and higher education policy. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The struggles of a perfect child | Ethan Pattoo | TEDxMiddlesex University Mauritius
recentItems.description: “We are not creating leaders of tomorrow, but the leaders of today.” This talk challenges the idea of the “perfect child” and reveals the hidden emotional cost of constantly meeting others’ expectations. It explores how perfectionism can create anxiety, burnout, and a fragile sense of self-worth built on achievement rather than identity. Through compelling examples, Ethan Pattoo, a final year secondary school student, highlights the importance of allowing young people to make mistakes, embrace uncertainty, and discover who they truly are.  Ethan Pattoo is a student at Westcoast International Secondary School in Mauritius. He is also a competitive judoka, representing the Akira Kai JC club This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Are you really choosing the books you read? | Krystabell Midiwo | TEDxMiddlesex University Mauritius
recentItems.description: The speaker explores how platforms like BookTok and social media algorithms are quietly shaping the books we read and the stories that become popular. The audience is set to think about whether algorithms are expanding our reading choices or keeping us stuck in familiar patterns. Blending examples from modern reading culture with the evolving publishing industry, Krystabell Midiwo highlights both the opportunities and limitations of algorithm-driven recommendations. recentItems.title: Acceptance as rebellion | Britney Soll | TEDxMiddlesex University Mauritius
recentItems.description: “Acceptance is not surrender nor is it passive resignation. Acceptance is rebellion because I know the world in all its dark places and limits, and still choose, within it, to do what matters.” This talk explores how courage is found not in avoiding pain, anxiety, or hardship, but in choosing how we respond to them. Through powerful personal stories, Britney Soll challenges us to distinguish between real limitations and the fears that only appear to confine us. Ultimately, it is a call to embrace life's uncertainties, heal from past wounds, and defiantly choose hope, love, and purpose. Britney Soll is currently studying a Doctorate in Counseling Psychology and Psychotherapy and she is better known in Mauritius for her work with therapy dogs, but she have been on the scientist-practitioner psychologist trajectory for the last 5 years. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The DNA of community development | Nancy Veerayen | TEDxMiddlesex University Mauritius
recentItems.description: Beyond our biological DNA, we all inherit a “social DNA” shaped by the communities we belong to. Using personal stories and lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr Nancy Veerayen demonstrates how communities influence our values, relationships, and sense of belonging. Through the framework of Diversity, Networks, and Action (DNA), she highlights the essential ingredients of thriving and inclusive communities. The talk ultimately challenges us to consider what kind of community legacy we are creating for future generations. Dr Nancy Veerayen is a British-qualified social worker specialising in international social work and community development. Her career before immigrating to Mauritius included working in child protection for UK social services. Immigrating to Mauritius, she represented Mauritius in 2005 at the British Treasury-sponsored Pan African InterAction Leadership Programme, 'Africa for Africa through Collaboration', in Kenya. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
